label: EDPB Guidelines 9/2022 on Personal Data Breach Notification
body: • Three breach categories: confidentiality (unauthorised disclosure/access), integrity (unauthorised alteration), availability (loss of access or destruction). Each demands its own risk analysis.
• "Awareness" under Art. 33(1) means having a reasonable degree of certainty that a security incident has occurred which led to personal data being compromised — not awaiting a full forensic report.

• Risk-assessment factors (carried over from WP250): type of breach; nature, sensitivity and volume of data; ease of identification of individuals; severity of consequences; special characteristics of the individuals and of the controller; number of affected individuals.
• Encrypted-data + uncompromised keys + working backups = often no SA notification; document the analysis in the breach register either way.
• Ransomware that only encrypts data (no exfiltration) is generally an availability breach; high-risk if it delays delivery of essential services (e.g. hospital).

• Processor must notify controller "without undue delay" (Art. 33(2)) — interpreted as immediately on becoming aware; the controller's 72h runs from controller awareness, which is normally triggered by the processor's notification.

• Cross-border breaches: an EU-established controller engaged in cross-border processing notifies the lead SA (Art. 56 one-stop-shop). A controller without an EU establishment cannot use the one-stop-shop — the presence of an Art. 27 representative does not create a lead SA — and must notify the SA of every member state where affected data subjects reside (the central revision 9/2022 made to WP250).

• Worked examples covering: stolen encrypted backup; misdirected email; ransomware on hospital; exfiltration of customer database; insider human-risk; social engineering. Each example walks through risk assessment + notification decision + records.
